title: Force-bearing skeletal muscle after volumetric muscle loss

concept.text: The proposed innovation is regeneration of durable, voluntarily controlled, force-producing skeletal muscle after substantial volumetric muscle loss (VML). It would replace missing contractile tissue with living muscle that receives adequate blood flow, responds to motor nerves and transmits force through appropriate mechanical attachments. Success would require coordinated restoration of muscle mass, structure and function.

VML can leave persistent losses of muscle mass and contractile strength because endogenous regeneration does not adequately replace the missing tissue. Fibrosis, vascular abnormalities and disrupted innervation complicate recovery. The intended capability would overcome these interacting limitations sufficiently to restore useful voluntary force; the supplied evidence does not establish that this has been achieved in humans after substantial VML.

significance.text: Restoring substantial muscle mass and voluntary force without sacrificing donor muscle would represent a major reconstructive capability beyond the modest clinical recovery described in the supplied evidence. Persistent weakness is a central consequence of VML, so durable strength restoration would directly address the injury's functional burden. The advance would be meaningful because the regenerated tissue contracts and contributes force, rather than merely occupying the defect.

Conditional applications: restored muscle force could improve gait, increase the usefulness of a salvaged limb, provide power for a tendon transfer or improve residual-limb function. These outcomes would also depend on the location of the defect, mechanical attachments, neural control, rehabilitation and other injuries. They are plausible downstream possibilities, not automatic consequences or demonstrated outcomes of the proposed innovation.

Scope synthesis: this capability would address one major component of limb function. It would not by itself establish regeneration of an amputated extremity, restoration of a destroyed joint or repair of a transected nerve trunk. Those distinctions limit how broadly successful muscle regeneration could be interpreted, especially in injuries involving several tissues.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is coordinated regeneration of enough functional muscle to restore durable voluntary force after a substantial tissue deficit. The barriers extend beyond generating muscle cells: viable contractile tissue must develop an effective architecture, receive adequate perfusion, acquire motor innervation and transmit its force to the remaining musculoskeletal system. Damage to nerves, vessels and myotendinous junctions varies between injuries, so the integration problem will also vary.

The injured environment itself can obstruct regeneration. The supplied review describes impaired extracellular-matrix remodeling that suppresses satellite-cell activation, alongside fibrosis, vascular dysfunction and denervation. Satellite cells therefore cannot be assumed to rebuild a large defect simply because they participate in normal muscle repair. A successful treatment would need to overcome the local conditions that prevent effective regeneration while establishing functional tissue integration.

The evidence does not establish a universal defect-size threshold above which muscle invariably heals with fibrosis. It also does not substantiate the original assertion about donor-site limitations of transferred muscle flaps. Avoiding donor-muscle sacrifice remains a proposed design objective, but the supplied record cannot quantify the comparative advantage over flap reconstruction.

current_state.text: Garg and colleagues' review, published online on 28 February 2025 in the Journal of Physiology, volume 603, pages 7421–7439, DOI 10.1113/JP286551, reports that only acellular extracellular-matrix scaffolds had been combined with physical therapy in VML-injured patients, with modest functional improvement. That statement concerns the scaffold-plus-physical-therapy approach described in the abstract; it does not establish that patients had received no other kinds of treatment. The supplied evidence for this article is a PubMed abstract record, not the full review, despite its untruncated extraction.

Sarah M. Greising and Jarrod A. Call's review was first published on 20 November 2025 and appeared in Experimental Physiology, volume 111, pages 1718–1732, in 2026, DOI 10.1113/EP093074. It describes persistent deficits after VML, partial preclinical recovery and continuing translational limitations, and states that full functional recovery remains elusive. The supplied validated review reports that the retained full-text XML identifies both authors and includes the article body and references without reported truncation, resolving the earlier incomplete author capture.

Together, these dated reviews support a continuing gap between partial recovery and durable restoration of reinnervated human muscle force after substantial VML. The supplied material does not document the earlier assertion that rat constructs produced early force gains that later converged with controls. That trajectory remains unverified here; its absence from this record does not establish that the underlying result is false.

Temporal limitation: the supplied bounded search record is empty. These sources support statements at their documented review dates, but they do not establish an exhaustive account of developments through 1 November 2026 or prove that no subsequent breakthrough occurred.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed human demonstration: enroll patients with an acute, prospectively defined substantial volumetric defect of a major limb muscle, such as the quadriceps. At two years, treatment would restore viable contractile muscle volume and voluntary torque to within a proposed 15% of an appropriate reference, demonstrate reinnervation by electromyography and avoid donor-muscle sacrifice. The 15% tolerance, two-year duration, acute setting and donor-sparing condition are proposed evaluation choices, not established standards or reported achievements.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed human demonstration

completion_criteria.text: Proposed measurement safeguards: define defect size, reference measurements and rehabilitation before treatment. Distinguish viable contractile tissue from fibrotic or other space-filling tissue, demonstrate adequate perfusion and show that the restored tissue contributes to mechanical force transmission. Torque recovery should be evaluated for compensation by surviving muscle. Contralateral measurements should be interpreted alongside preinjury measurements where available and suitable external reference data.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed measurement safeguards

completion_criteria.text: The rationale for prioritizing force, mass, structure and reinnervation follows from the documented deficits and the review's emphasis on contraction and force production as the principal function of muscle. The review's caution about contralateral controls concerned mouse mitochondrial respiration; it supports careful reference selection but does not itself invalidate human contralateral torque comparisons.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: reproduce substantial functional restoration in independent patient cohorts with clearly described defect locations, sizes, associated injuries and rehabilitation. Report durability, safety and the conditions under which recovery fails or remains incomplete. A scaffold that fills space and produces only a small strength gain would not meet this proposed endpoint. Success in an acute quadriceps defect would establish demonstrated breadth within the tested conditions; chronic scarred defects, other muscles and injuries with major nerve or attachment loss would require additional evidence.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries

related_concepts.text: Roster-based scope synthesis: ORT-01, Adult epimorphic regeneration of a functional limb, encompasses a much broader reconstruction problem in which functional muscle would be one necessary component. ORT-06 concerns replacement of missing muscle within an existing limb and would not establish whole-limb regeneration. ORT-07, Meaningful motor and sensory recovery across long peripheral-nerve gaps, overlaps through the need for effective neural control, but muscle reinnervation does not demonstrate repair across a long nerve gap or recovery of sensory function.

Roster-based scope synthesis: ORT-04, Regeneration of the load-bearing tendon–bone enthesis, concerns the attachment through which tendon transfers load to bone. ORT-06 needs effective force transmission, but generating contractile muscle would not by itself regenerate an injured enthesis. ORT-02, Biological restoration of the osteoarthritic synovial joint, addresses a separate joint-level barrier to limb function. ORT-05, Restoration of the intervertebral disc as a living load-bearing organ, shares the broad goal of functional tissue restoration while targeting a different anatomical structure and mechanical role.

Roster-based scope synthesis: ORT-10, Single-episode restoration of segmental long bone by vascularized, remodelable bone, could complement muscle reconstruction in a combined bone-and-muscle defect. ORT-08, Anatomically precise and reversible control of osteogenesis, concerns control of bone formation rather than muscle regeneration. ORT-09, Regeneration of a functioning growth plate, targets skeletal growth. Success in any one of these capabilities would not establish the others.

Roster-based scope synthesis: ORT-03, Eradication of mature biofilm in bone and on orthopedic implants without removing the reconstruction, could matter when muscle reconstruction accompanies an infected orthopedic injury. Its defining endpoint is infection eradication while retaining the reconstruction; ORT-06's defining endpoint is regenerated muscle force. The capabilities remain distinct even when both are needed in the same patient.

change_log.change: Preserved ORT-06's identity and expanded the explanation around durable voluntary force, perfusion, innervation, architecture and mechanical integration.
change_log.reason: The research and review jointly define a coordinated functional reconstruction capability, not simply replacement of tissue volume.

change_log.change: Replaced the universal small-defect threshold with evidence-grounded descriptions of persistent deficits, fibrosis and impaired satellite-cell activation.
change_log.reason: The supplied evidence supports these mechanisms but does not establish a universal size cutoff.

change_log.change: Qualified donor-flap limitations and retained donor-muscle preservation as a proposed objective.
change_log.reason: The supplied record does not document donor-site limitations or quantify a comparative benefit.

change_log.change: Separated direct strength restoration from conditional gait, tendon-transfer, residual-limb and whole-limb benefits.
change_log.reason: Those applications depend on anatomy, attachments, neural control and associated injuries.

unresolved_issues: The supplied evidence does not verify the claimed early-to-late convergence of rat construct force gains with controls.
Developments after the dated reviews, including the latest state as of 1 November 2026, remain unverified.
A universal defect-size threshold and the asserted donor-site limitations of muscle-flap reconstruction are not established by the supplied record.
The proposed human endpoint still requires protocol-specific definitions of substantial defect size, viable contractile volume, reference values and attribution of recovered force.
The proposed 15% tolerance and two-year duration have not been established here as consensus thresholds.
Benefits for gait, tendon transfers and residual limbs remain conditional applications requiring direct evaluation.
Related-concept comparisons rely on the supplied roster titles rather than detailed evidence reviews of those entries.
